chapters.relation: This introductory prospectus argues that fictional narrative films (and their makers) can 'do' philosophy, and proposes Joss Whedon's corpus as a surprising confirming instance of the film-as-philosophy thesis. It defines philosophy as an activity of asking universal questions and removing contradictions by argument, then chapter-by-chapter previews how Buffy, Angel, Firefly/Serenity, Dr. Horrible, Dollhouse, The Cabin in the Woods and the Avengers films will be read through Heidegger, Sartre, Socrates, Rawls, Plato, Aristotle, Locke, Kant, Mill, Parfit and others. It sets out the interpretive presuppositions (what counts as Whedon 'canon') that govern the whole book.

chapters.file: ch06 - The Peculiarities of Free Will.md
chapters.relation: This file collects Part I chapters 1-5. It argues Whedon's heroes (Angel, Buffy, Spike, Simon, Echo, Captain America) achieve authentic selfhood by resisting depersonalizing forces, reading their 'angst' through Heidegger and Sartre while insisting Whedon is more Socratic than existentialist because he affirms objective goods, synthesized via a Rawlsian just society. It then adds Aristotle on friendship and community (Toy Story, Jayne, Angel's team) and defends an atheistic ethics grounding natural rights in Locke and Kant plus Aristotelian virtue (Spike's re-ensoulment), using the Euthyphro to reject divine-command theory. The title chapter argues Whedon's paradoxical portrayal of free will in The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse and Cabin fits neither hard determinism nor compatibilism but Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions.

chapters.file: ch07 - Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity.md
chapters.relation: This file collects Part II chapters 6-9. It defends Stephen Mulhall's 'bold thesis' against Baggini, Murray Smith and Livingston, using Whedon's dialogue-free episode 'Hush' as film that 'shows' a Zen-like epistemic point resisting paraphrase, and works through the Russell-Wartenberg debate over whether narrative film can convey arguments (via The Matrix and Eternal Sunshine). It reads The Cabin in the Woods as a counterargument to utilitarianism grounded in Nel Noddings's ethics of care ('people are more important than humanity') and an Aristotelian theory of worthwhile horror. The Angel/Angelus chapter stages the Wes-Holtz dispute as competing theories of personal identity, testing Locke's memory theory and Parfit's psychological-continuity view against Whedon's soul-based metaphysics to argue what ultimately matters is one's care-based relations with others.
